title: Signatures of nodal superconductivity in stoichiometric FeTe
authors: Cequn Li, Zi-Jie Yan, Yang Ge, Zihao Wang, Bing Xia, Stephen Paolini, Pu Xiao, Lok-Kan Lai, Jiatao Song, Austin R. Kaczmarek, Lujin Min, Kenji Yasuda, Peter J. Hirschfeld, Jiabin Yu, Cui-Zu Chang, Katja C. Nowack
abstract: Superconductivity in stoichiometric FeTe opens access to the FeTe endpoint of the Fe(Se,Te) phase diagram, yet the nature of its superconducting pairing state remains unresolved. In this work, we combine scanning superconducting quantum interference device (SQUID) microscopy, electrical transport, scanning tunneling microscopy and spectroscopy (STM/S), and mean-field calculations to investigate the local superfluid response and pairing state of FeTe thin films with tunable stoichiometry. Even in stoichiometric FeTe, we observe micrometer-scale spatial variations in both superfluid stiffness and superconducting transition temperature $T_c$, while the London penetration depth remains non-saturating down to 0.02$T_c$ and follows a power-law temperature dependence with an exponent of approximately 1-1.5. Together with a V-shaped low-energy density of states and two-gap modeling, these results indicate a superconducting state with gap nodes or deep minima, consistent with either a $d$-wave or nodal $s$-wave superconducting state. Our findings establish stoichiometric FeTe as a distinct superconducting regime that departs from the trend toward more isotropic gaps at intermediate Se/Te compositions, providing a new benchmark for modern microscopic theories of iron-chalcogenide superconductivity. Our work also reveals a crossover from weak to rapid suppression of $T_c$ as superfluid stiffness decreases, connecting FeTe to the broader phenomenology observed in unconventional superconductors.
summary: This work investigates the superconducting pairing symmetry in stoichiometric FeTe using a combination of SQUID microscopy, STM spectroscopy, and mean-field theory. Experimental results point towards a nodal superconducting state characterized by power-law temperature dependencies, which is theoretically reproduced by modeling the system with specific attractive interactions leading to nodal d-wave or nodal s-wave pairing.
main_problem: To determine the nature of the superconducting pairing state in stoichiometric FeTe and whether it deviates from the isotropic gap trend seen in intermediate Fe(Se,Te) compositions.
main_result: Experimental evidence (power-law $\lambda(T)$ and V-shaped DOS) strongly suggests a nodal superconducting state (d-wave or nodal s-wave), which is theoretically supported by mean-field calculations incorporating specific attractive interactions.
method: The study combines multiple experimental techniques (SQUID, STM/S, transport) with theoretical modeling using mean-field calculations on an effective Hamiltonian.
model_or_system: The system is stoichiometric FeTe thin films. Theoretically, it is modeled using a Hubbard-Kanamori Hamiltonian solved via mean-field theory, incorporating various attractive interactions (NN, NNN, NNNN) to stabilize different pairing symmetries.
key_observables: Superfluid stiffness ($\kappa_s$), London penetration depth ($\lambda(T)$), low-energy density of states (DOS), and the superconducting transition temperature ($T_c$).
important_parameters: The superconducting gap structure (nodal vs. fully gapped), the temperature dependence exponents ($n \approx 1.2$ for $ho_s(T)$), and interaction parameters ($U, V_2, V_3, V_4$).
main_assumptions: The SQUID measurement assumes the Pearl limit ($\lambda \gg d$), and the theoretical analysis uses mean-field approximations while preserving certain symmetries (SU(2), time-reversal).
figures_summary: Figures show spatial maps of superfluid stiffness and $T_c$ inhomogeneity, power-law fits for $ho_s(T)$ and $\Delta\lambda/\lambda(0)$, and theoretical DOS plots comparing nodal d-wave and nodal s-wave predictions against experimental STS data.
paper_structure: The paper progresses from experimental characterization of spatial inhomogeneity and power-law temperature dependencies (SQUID/STM) to theoretical modeling using mean-field theory to reproduce the observed nodal gap signatures.
why_interesting: The combination of advanced experimental diagnostics (SQUID, STM) with detailed theoretical modeling of pairing symmetries in iron-based superconductors provides a rich playground for understanding unconventional pairing mechanisms beyond simple BCS theory.

The response is spatially inhomogeneous, revealing nearly twofold varia- tions in the superfluid stiffness across the field of view, with darker regions corresponding to stronger superfluid stiffness.
